Prevention: Resistant varieties available are the best means of controlling common smut.
Rotate with non-cereals and plough deep.
Maintain well-balanced soil fertility based on a soil test.
Avoid mechanical injuries to plants during cultivation and spraying.
Avoid injury of roots, stalks, and leaves during cultivation.
Protect corn against insects (such as corn earworms and corn borers) by timely applications of insecticides.
Maize is very sensitive to weed competition during the first 4-6 weeks after emergence.
Avoid irrigation water coming into the field from an infected field.
Monitoring: Scout the field two or three times a week during the earing stage of maize.
Inspect the inflorescence of the plant to look for black powder.
The corn plant may be infected at any time in the early stages of growth but becomes less susceptible after the formation of the ear.
Corn smut overwinters on debris and in the soil.
It is carried by wind, rain and irrigation and does best in hot, dry weather.
Spores may remain viable for 5 to 7 years.
Direct Control: The removal of the smut should always be accompanied by long crop rotations.
Cutting out all the smut balls before they have time to break open and destroying them by burial or fire, could reduce smut.
One year of cutting is not enough to cause a noticeable difference in the amount of the disease, but if this cutting is continued for 2 or more years, the smut will gradually be reduced.
Do not compost infected plant parts.
Restrictions: Copper and sulphur fungicides are toxic for aquatic life and mammals.
Always spray under the recommendations of labels.
Spray weekly when the disease is first noticed and continue the applications as long as the disease conditions are favourable.
